israeli-integration-into-us-agencies.title: Israeli integration into U.S. agencies
israeli-integration-into-us-agencies.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to the formal embedding of Israeli personnel inside American defense and intelligence institutions — a National Defense Authorization Act provision collocating them with the Pentagon and opening Five Eyes-style liaison with the CIA, arriving in the same weeks as a DIA all-hands warning that Israeli services were unusually aggressive in recruiting inside DIA. His argument is that the two cannot both be true: either Israel is a critical counterintelligence threat or it is a partner.

data.Effect (per Kiriakou): Collocation with the Pentagon; Five Eyes-style CIA liaison
data.Contemporaneous warning: DIA director's all-hands email on Israeli recruitment inside DIA
data.Kiriakou's objection: 'Either… or. But it can't be both'

dyk: … that a National Defense Authorization Act provision would seat Israeli personnel alongside the Pentagon with [Five Eyes](/wiki/five-eyes)-style [CIA](/wiki/cia) liaison — in the same weeks the DIA director warned staff that Israeli services were trying to recruit inside DIA?

… that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) notes Israel belongs to neither NATO nor the EU — and that if it attacked Turkey as its defence minister threatened, Article 5 would oblige the United States to fight [Israel](/wiki/israel-united-states-relations)?
israeli-integration-into-us-agencies.body:
**Israeli integration into U.S. agencies** is the subject of an argument [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) makes from an internal contradiction rather than from policy preference. Asked in July 2026 whether the United States still has a [CIA](/wiki/cia) of its own, he set two contemporaneous facts against each other.

The first is legislative. A provision of the National Defense Authorization Act for 2027 — numbered 219, and previously 224 — would collocate Israeli personnel with the Pentagon and permit closer, *"five eyes style"* liaison with the CIA. Kiriakou notes that an earlier attempt was made without a vote, and that the opposition in Congress amounts to [Thomas Massie](/wiki/thomas-massie), Ro Khanna and a handful of others.<Cite t="35:05" /><Cite t="50:15" />

The second is counterintelligence. Two weeks before the interview, NBC News reported that the director of the Defense Intelligence Agency had sent an all-hands email warning that the Israelis were *"being unusually aggressive right now in trying to recruit assets inside DIA"* and that every employee should be extra careful.<Cite t="35:36" />

Kiriakou's objection is that both cannot stand: *"Either the Israelis are ranked as critical threat for counter intelligence, which is what they were when I was there, along with the Russians, the Chinese, the Cubans, and the North Koreans, or we're joined at the hip. But it can't be both."*<Cite t="36:07" />

## What changed

He sets the present arrangement against the one he entered. When he joined the CIA the agency *"did not like the Israelis at all. They were spying on us. They made it clear. They openly spied on us"* — and brought gifts with listening devices embedded in them, to the point that Israeli officers were barred from the headquarters building entirely and the agency rented space elsewhere for liaison meetings.<Cite t="34:33" />

Asked what changed — whether it is blackmail — Kiriakou says the answer is *"broader and more nefarious than that,"* and political rather than personal. Arab leaders have told him, and told American ambassadors in his hearing, that the last U.S. president to give the Arabs a fair shake was George H. W. Bush; they also remember Kennedy and Eisenhower. Since then the pressure has been incremental, exerted through the White House and through [AIPAC](/wiki/aipac) on Capitol Hill, until *"if you disagree not just with Israeli policy, if you disagree with [Benjamin Netanyahu](/wiki/benjamin-netanyahu) as a person, you are labeled as anti-Semitic. Of course it took them decades to get to that point, but they did it."*<Cite t="36:40" /><Cite t="37:12" /><Cite t="37:44" />

## Why he says merging militaries is not routine

Against the claim that the United States routinely merges its military with allies', Kiriakou draws the boundary at the [Five Eyes](/wiki/five-eyes): the British, Canadians, Australians and New Zealanders. Israel is a member of neither NATO nor the European Union.<Cite t="39:20" /><Cite t="39:51" />

He then puts a case he treats as decisive. Israel's defence minister had said publicly that Israel's next war would be against Turkey — and Turkey is in NATO. If hostilities followed and Turkey invoked Article 5, the United States would be treaty-bound to go to war with Israel. *"Is the United States going to go to war with Israel? Of course not. And so what happens? The Israelis then successfully destroy NATO."*<Cite t="40:21" />

On the espionage itself his standard is comparative: technology theft on this scale by any other country *"would have us on the brink of war with them right now."*<Cite t="38:48" /> The [F-35 avionics dispute](/wiki/f-35-israel-avionics) is the example he reaches for.<Cite t="52:18" />

## Police training

A form of integration already in place, Kiriakou notes, receives almost no mainstream coverage: Israeli police and IDF personnel training American police departments, including in Atlanta at the training facility known as Cop City. His objection is categorical — *"I don't want the Israelis training American police departments. The Israelis have no respect for human rights or civil rights or civil liberties"* — and he frames the wider question as whether this is a country to throw in with, given that it *"has bombed seven of its neighbors in the past year."*<Cite t="49:14" /><Cite t="49:44" />

## Where he thinks it ends

Asked how it stops, Kiriakou sets aside the optimism he says he is usually accused of. Every incremental change across thirty-five years has run in Israel's favour, and although polling now shows a clear majority of Americans saying the relationship is too close and that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, elected officials have not moved with them: roughly 77 percent of Democratic voters say they support the Palestinian side against about 90 percent of elected Democrats supporting Israel. The handful willing to break ranks does not grow. *"And where does that leave us? That leaves us in a place where we don't have a democracy."*<Cite t="56:25" /><Cite t="56:56" /><Cite t="57:28" />

kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.title: Kiriakou and Cenk Uygur
kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.summary: A grievance John Kiriakou carried for a decade — that Cenk Uygur had spent thirty minutes attacking him over his first letter from prison — resolved live on air in July 2026 when Uygur produced his archive, found no such segment, and both men concluded it had been mistaken identity.

data.The grievance: A remembered 30-minute on-air attack over the first letter from Loretto
data.The occasion: Kiriakou's open letter to supporters from prison; Jake Tapper interviewed him there
data.Resolution: No such segment exists in the archive; mistaken identity, apologised on air

dyk: … that [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) resented Cenk Uygur for a decade over a broadcast attack on his [first letter from prison](/wiki/fci-loretto) — until Uygur searched the archive on air and found it had never happened?

… that the letter at the centre of it — [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou)'s open letter from [FCI Loretto](/wiki/fci-loretto) — was the piece that brought [Jake Tapper](/wiki/jake-tapper) to the prison to interview him?
kiriakou-and-cenk-uygur.body:
**Kiriakou and Cenk Uygur** describes a decade-long grievance that turned out to rest on nothing, and which the two men resolved on air in July 2026.

The occasion Kiriakou remembered was the second thing he did after blowing the whistle that drew wide press coverage: an open letter to his supporters written from prison, the first of what became his letters from [FCI Loretto](/wiki/fci-loretto). It was that letter, he says, that brought [Jake Tapper](/wiki/jake-tapper) to the prison to interview him. *"The response was universally positive and interested — except for Cenk Uygur. Cenk Uygur just for 30 minutes just ripped me."*<Cite t="31:57" /><Cite t="32:27" />

What made it stick was that Kiriakou could not account for it. *"I never understood that, because back then I probably agreed on 95% of the issues with Cenk Uygur. Like, why is he attacking me like this?"*<Cite t="32:27" /> Uygur's account of the relationship from the other side was similar in shape: he had wanted the friendship and never got a reply. *"It's like an unrequited romance where you're sort of like, we should be buds, we agree about a lot of stuff — and then they never call, they never write."*<Cite t="32:58" />

The resolution came from the archive. Uygur said he had become obsessed with identifying the segment, searched the show's records, and found that *"no such thing exists"* — concluding it must have been mistaken identity, and that *"maybe there is a Cenk Uygur out there somewhere who did attack you."* Kiriakou apologised: *"I want to apologize for that, because I think I must have been temporarily insane or something."*<Cite t="33:29" />

The episode is a small illustration of a point Kiriakou makes at length elsewhere about manufactured or misremembered antagonism, and it framed an interview in which the two found themselves in agreement throughout. Uygur closed it by noting the composition of the panel — *"here's a Turk, a Greek, and an Armenian"* — all arguing not for Turkey, Greece or Armenia but for the United States.<Cite t="1:02:08" />
